releases.body:
**One identity per conversation, held for a window.** The `(project id, session id)` pair is no longer minted per request. `currentIdentity` keeps one pair per conversation for `OPENCODE_ZEN_FREE_IDENTITY_TTL_MS` — 60 seconds by default — and replaces both halves together when the window ends. The slot is `conversationKey`, a digest of the host's own name for the conversation, read by the same ladder `sessionID` walks: the session header the CLI already sends on every request, then the body's `conversation_id`, `metadata.session_id` or Claude Code user id. The name itself is never sent — only the pair minted for it — so keying by it costs nothing at the tier and keeps two conversations from sharing one session, one memory and one refusal.

**Why a window rather than a request.** A burst of requests that each hop to a fresh identity is refused as a batch, where the same requests spaced about half a second apart pass; a client that appears as a hundred strangers in a minute is a client the gate has an opinion about. Holding a pair is also the shape a real client has — it opens a conversation, uses it for a while, opens another. `OPENCODE_ZEN_FREE_IDENTITY_TTL_MS=0` restores the per-request minting this package shipped with, which is also the value to measure a ledger with: an id that rotates cannot answer a question about one id. The opening and `previous_response_id` are deliberately not names — the opening moves when a host shortens its history and a continuation id is new on every turn, so keyed by either a conversation would answer a new pair every turn. A request that names nothing shares the unnamed slot, which is the single pair this package used before the window existed.

**A refusal is one conversation's business.** A 429 rotates only the slot it refused (`rotateIdentity`), and the pair that answered becomes that conversation's window, because a ledger proven to answer is worth more than the one it replaced. Session affinity still owns both halves when it is set, and a project id the host named is never re-minted; the window is this package's own bookkeeping and moves only what this package minted. The ledger map is bounded at 1000 conversations, least recently used out.

**The bound the docs used to state is now in doubt.** MAINTAINING recorded that one fixed project id served ~15M tokens without a refusal, and read that as "the egress budget is almost always the one that answers". On 2026-10-28 an operator reported a spent tier answering again after the local state was wiped *and* the egress replaced — which the two-budget model does not predict, since a fresh egress is already a fresh `(id, egress)` pair. Either the wipe was not what recovered it, or an id-level budget exists that the 15M run never reached. One experiment tells the two apart: change only the egress and keep the id. Until that is run, the 15M figure is the floor of an unmeasured quantity, not a statement that no id-level cap exists.

853 tests pass under Bun (16 files, 0 fail).

**The protocol catalogue, and two watchers that say when OpenCode has moved.** `catalog.mjs` keeps a snapshot of which endpoint each model is served at — parsed from OpenCode's docs page by `models-watch.mjs --sweep --write`, preflighted by `--check`, and published hourly by `catalog.yml` through the pull request automerge merges. Discovery answers from the live docs, then the discovery cache, then the remote snapshot, then the bundled copy, then the bootstrap table in code; a restart keeps the floor while offline. `releases-watch.mjs` reads OpenCode's releases feed against the version `fingerprint.json` says it was captured from and answers 0 / 1 / 2; a newer release opens the one issue that asks for a capture, and the watcher itself rewrites nothing. Its first run caught a real one: 2.2.0 was published against a 2.1.4 fingerprint.

**The capture follows it to 2.2.0.** A desktop build only runs its own server when given `--standalone`; without it the run printed its banner and left with no request sent. `capture` passes the flag now (the stock CLI ignores it), and the fingerprint moved to `opencode/latest/2.2.0/desktop` — the client segment said `cli` on 2.1.4 — with `read` and `shell` carrying `additionalProperties: false`. The prompt came through byte for byte unchanged and all twelve tools match `official-tools.json` exactly, so nothing was rewritten by hand; the one new block, the skill listing, is the one `official-prompt.mjs` strips. The raw request is kept beside its predecessor as `genuine-2.2.0-request.json`.

**A promptless request earns the same 429 as a spent quota.** Every gate run on 2026-10-28 read `HTTP 429` four times, on two egresses, under fresh and established session ids, on three models, while the conversation beside it ran on the same tier without one. The bisection landed on the one thing the probes lacked: the system prompt. A promptless request — whatever its tools, its ids, its egress — is refused with the same `FreeUsageLimitError` a spent quota earns; the verbatim replay of a genuine request answers 200, and so does the same tiny probe carrying only the system message. `chatRequest` sends the generation's prompt now, and `retry-after` is quoted in full rather than dropped when the body runs long.

**Three knobs, each off by default.** `OPENCODE_ZEN_FREE_RETRY_AFTER=1` hands one attempt's wait to the `retry-after` window a 429 names, bounded like every wait here at 120 s and read in both spellings HTTP gives it. `OPENCODE_ZEN_FREE_PACING_MS` spaces this loader's own consecutive requests — the burst shape zen-proxy measured the gate blanket-refusing where the same requests half a second apart pass. And a retry mints its `(session, project)` replacement as one pair from one clock reading (`mintIdentity`), which is what the tier reads as one ledger.

**Docs, and a test that expired.** MAINTAINING gains the watchers' section, the 2.2.0 capture as the worked example the releases watcher promises, the 429 body's second meaning, and the three knobs. `make-llms.mjs` writes `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt` from the English README and MAINTAINING — the machine-readable pair zen-proxy keeps — and both READMEs link them. `limits-watch.test.mjs`'s `goodRow` carried `2026-10-20` in the source; the day it crossed the seven-day bound the row-freshness check enforces, the suite went red on a constant. The one case that runs against the real clock names its own day now.

841 tests pass under Bun in CI (16 files, 0 fail); the four affected suites also pass under Node 26 (8 capture tests skipped, as they want Bun).

**A cut stream is named as one.** When the upstream closed an SSE stream mid-reply, the guard told the client `Upstream request failed` — true, and unclassifiable. A host that reads the text to decide whether asking again can help has no class for it; DeepSeek Harness, for one, reads `stream ended before|without` as a transport failure and retries it, while the bare sentence fell outside every class its policy names, so the turn ended. The synthesized failure now says the shape the client got: `Upstream request failed: the stream ended before the reply was complete`. The guard's own truncation failures say the same thing in the same words: an event cut in the middle now ends with `Upstream SSE stream ended before an event was complete`, and a stream that closed without its terminal ends with `Upstream SSE stream ended without a completion marker (...)`. The collapse path's completion-marker sentence moves with them, so both readings of one stream answer the same words. None of them says anything about the cause; the raw failure stays in the server's log. Measured against dsh's installed `classifyPiAiError`: the old sentences are `PI_AI_ERROR`, the new ones `TRANSPORT`, and `TRANSPORT` is in the default retryable codes.


827 tests pass under Bun in CI; the three affected suites pass under Node 26 as well.

Two changes: a fix for a knob that never worked, and a correction to what a 429 is about.

**Session affinity is now real (PR #11, thanks @dgqyushen).** `OPENCODE_ZEN_FREE_SESSION_AFFINITY=1` is documented to keep one session per conversation. It never did: `attempts += 1` ran before the headers were built, so the `attempts === 0` branch that keeps the chosen session never matched, and every attempt minted a fresh one. Invisible in the default mode — both sides are fresh ids there — which is how it shipped. The counter now moves after the headers exist: the first attempt opens under the conversation's session, and only a retry mints one nothing has spent. A new test pins all three states; it fails against the old code and passes with the fix.

**The 429 ledger, measured again.** The `public` credential identifies no one, so quota has nothing to do with the key: it is ledgered per egress IP, with per-(project id × egress) ledgers beneath it. On 2026-10-27, an exit whose admission probe had just answered 200 refused a ~32k-token request five times and then a ~5k one five more — twenty fresh project ids, one answer, while our own spend on that IP was ~10k tokens. On a saturated exit no fresh id opens a ledger; only time helps. The other arm of the model is bounded too: one fixed project id served ~15M tokens across seventeen exits without a refusal, so the id ledger is not what a 429 is about. README, README.en, MAINTAINING and .env.example now say this.

node --test: 807 pass (the 8 capture tests want Bun).

0.5.11 waited 1200 ms, then 2400 ms, and gave up. That is the right shape for a host with nothing behind a 429 — the bucket is spent and a longer wait only postpones the same answer.

The ceiling is configurable because a deployment may know that a longer wait is worth spending.

- `OPENCODE_ZEN_FREE_RETRY_WAIT_MAX_MS` is new: it raises the ceiling the doubling stops at (default still `5000`, ceiling `120000`).
- It is floored at the first wait (`OPENCODE_ZEN_FREE_RETRY_WAIT_MS`), so the two cannot be set to contradict each other and the backoff can never shrink.
- **Every default is unchanged.** A host that sets nothing gets exactly what 0.5.11 gave it: 2 retries, 1200 ms, ceiling 5000 ms.
- Out-of-range values fall back to the default rather than reaching the timer.

node --test 823 pass (the 8 capture tests want Bun).
